high_priority_articles.title: India-Mexico trade deal: Talks to begin this week amid fresh 50% tariffs on Indian exports | India News - Hindustan Times
high_priority_articles.summary: India-Mexico trade deal: Talks to begin this week amid fresh 50% tariffs on Indian exports | India News  Hindustan Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
India’s merchandise exports to Mexico stood at $5.73 billion in 2025-26, with automobiles accounting for the largest share at $1.92 billion.
India and Mexico will sign the terms of reference (ToR) this week to formally launch negotiations for a preferential trade agreement (PTA), aiming to protect Indian exports from recently imposed high tariffs in the Mexican market, officials said.
The proposed agreement is expected to cover key Indian exports, including automobiles, textiles, footwear, plastics, steel, chemicals and toys, which face tariffs of up to 50% under Mexico’s new tariff regime.
Both countries have finalised the terms of reference and are expected to sign the document in the next couple of days, the officials said, requesting anonymity. Commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal is visiting Mexico from Monday as part of a week-long trade mission that also includes Brussels, the headquarters of the European Union.
The proposed India-Mexico PTA is expected to help Indian exporters mitigate the impact of higher tariffs imposed by the Mexican government on 1,463 items imported from countries that do not have a bilateral trade arrangement with Mexico, such as a PTA or a free trade agreement (FTA).
Experts said signing the terms of reference would mark the first step towards protecting Indian exporters from the higher duties, particularly in the automobile sector.
According to government trade data, India’s merchandise exports to Mexico stood at $5.73 billion in 2025-26, with automobiles accounting for the largest share at $1.92 billion.
The list of products affected by Mexico’s tariff measures includes automobiles, textiles and clothing, plastics, steel, household appliances, aluminium, toys, furniture, footwear, leather goods, paper and cardboard, motorcycles, trailers and glass products.
The tariff measures took effect on January 1 under a decree linked to Mexico’s Plan, which aims to increase domestic content in production chains by 15% by 2030. Launched in January 2025, the initiative seeks to make Mexico one of the world’s 10 largest economies by 2030, revive local industries and create 1.5 million jobs.
PTA seen as faster route to protect exports
Experts said negotiating a bilateral PTA could help India address the tariff challenge more quickly than pursuing a comprehensive FTA, which would take relatively more time to conclude.
One official said the proposed agreement is expected to focus exclusively on preferential trade in goods.
A PTA generally has a limited scope and provides a positive list of products on which tariffs are reduced, though they are rarely eliminated entirely. An FTA, by contrast, seeks to eliminate tariffs on a much wider range of goods, subject to a negative list of excluded items.
India-Mexico trade stood at $7.83 billion in FY26
Bilateral merchandise trade between India and Mexico stood at around $7.83 billion in 2025-26, according to government data.
India exported goods worth approximately $5.73 billion to Mexico during the financial year, while imports from the Latin American country stood at $2.1 billion.
India’s major exports to Mexico include automobiles and auto parts, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and chemical products.
Mexico’s exports to India are dominated by crude oil, which accounts for almost three-fourths of its total shipments to the country. Other products supplied by Mexico include gold and related jewellery, as well as chemical compounds.
The proposed PTA is expected to provide a framework for preferential market access for selected goods, with negotiations set to begin following the formal signing of the terms of reference.

high_priority_articles.title: India's textile industry targets $350 billion by 2030 as exports rebound, costs rise: Report - ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.summary: India's textile industry targets $350 billion by 2030 as exports rebound, costs rise: Report  ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The sector reached nearly $190 billion in FY26, with exports rebounding 10.3% in April-August 2026, even as rising cotton yarn prices and US trade uncertainty weigh on manufacturers.
The report noted that the sector remains a primary employment generator while the central government considers a ₹400 billion, five-year Textile Expansion and Employment (TEEM) Scheme to upgrade machinery, deploy advanced technology, and modernise traditional clusters.
The expansion comes as outbound shipments rebound. Textile exports, including handicrafts, grew by 10.3 per cent year-on-year in the April-August 2026 period. The recovery follows a 2.7 per cent decline to $35.8 billion in FY2026, even as imports climbed 17.1 per cent to $9.6 billion.
Tushar Bhaskar, President of Rubix Data Sciences, noted that the sector continues to navigate external headwinds alongside domestic growth.
"India's textile industry has shown resilience, with exports growing 10.3% in April-August 2026 after a 2.7% decline in Dollar terms in FY2026," Bhaskar said.
"At the same time, trade uncertainty in the US market, a rise of approximately 60% in cotton yarn prices, and freight disruptions are adding to the pressure," he added. "This reinforces the importance of diversifying India's export destinations and improving cost competitiveness."
According to the report, the United States remained India's largest destination, taking 31 per cent of shipments in FY2026, followed by the European Union at nearly 16 per cent. However, trade dynamics shifted after the US introduced an additional 10 per cent duty under Section 301 measures in July 2026 concerning forced-labour enforcement, while broader negotiations stalled.
In response, domestic manufacturers accelerated market diversification. Shipments to the US fell approximately 7 per cent in FY2026, while deliveries to major European markets grew 9 per cent. Raymond Lifestyle plans to reduce its US export share from 65 per cent to between 55 and 60 per cent within two years, while Kitex Garments plans to lower its exposure from nearly 100 per cent to between 30 and 35 per cent over the next two to three years.
Input cost inflation also affected the domestic value chain. Cotton yarn prices climbed roughly 60 per cent to ₹400 per kilogram in September 2026 from ₹250 per kilogram in early 2026. The increase coincided with local cotton production dropping to 290.91 lakh bales in the 2025-26 season, down from 352.48 lakh bales in 2020-21. To assist mills, authorities granted an exemption on the 11 per cent cotton import duty through October 31, 2026.
Industrial infrastructure activity provided capital momentum. Investment proposals under the seven approved PM Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel Parks reached ₹685.9 billion by August 2026, led by major expansion outlays from corporate producers including Grasim Industries and Vardhman Textiles.

Egypt’s parliament authorized Monday military support for Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi attacks, following a request from President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi.
The House of Representatives "approved authorizing President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," state newspaper Al-Ahram reported.
The parliament, stacked with supporters of el-Sissi, had held three rare secret meetings on the matter and postponed the vote twice.
The president last week had asked parliament to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, "if requested."
It was not immediately clear what defensive support could be provided by Egypt, the Arab world's largest military, which boasts hundreds of thousands of active personnel, fighter jets and complex air defenses sourced from countries including the U.S., China, France and Russia.
El-Sissi said Wednesday that his country's support would be to "defend Saudi territory and does not include an attack on Yemen."
"We are talking about defending the land and borders of the kingdom," he said in a speech, adding that the top priority was for a diplomatic solution.
Egypt has undertaken a flurry of diplomatic maneuvers since, with Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty consulting with the so-called R4, which includes members of the Mecca defense pact, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, which Cairo has not agreed to join.
On Monday, he said he was "talking daily with the Iranians" to push for regional de-escalation.

high_priority_articles.summary: FOMC Meeting Puts Fed Interest Rate Decision in Focus as Inflation Rises  Coinpedia
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve faces a difficult decision ahead of its October 28 meeting as rising inflation and higher energy prices coincide with concerns about economic growth. Markets expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged, but Chair Kevin Warsh’s comments will be closely watched for clues about future rate decisions.
US inflation accelerated in September, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rising 3.7% year over year. The Producer Price Index (PPI), which measures changes in prices received by businesses, increased 1.3% from August. Higher energy prices have added to inflation concerns, while the US-Iran conflict has raised further uncertainty over energy costs.
Inflation and Economic Weakness Complicate Fed Policy
The Fed aims to bring inflation down to its 2% target, but higher energy costs could slow that progress. At the same time, high borrowing costs are weighing on housing affordability, and job cuts have raised concerns about employment.
This leaves policymakers balancing two risks. Keeping interest rates high could help control inflation but put further pressure on economic activity. Cutting rates could support growth but risk keeping inflation elevated.
These conditions have raised concerns about stagflation, which occurs when high inflation coincides with weak economic growth. Whether the US economy faces a sustained period of stagflation will depend on how prices, employment, and economic output develop.
Expectations of another rate increase at the October meeting have declined after New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson indicated that policymakers could take time to assess the economy following September’s rate increase.
Bloomberg Federal Reserve reporter Maria Luisa Capora said investors will focus on Warsh’s explanation for the expected pause and any indications about future policy.
Fed Guidance and Economic Data in Focus
Warsh’s comments could influence expectations for interest rates. A signal that rates may remain high for longer could put pressure on stocks, while indications of potential rate cuts could raise concerns about whether the Fed is doing enough to control inflation.
Investors will also watch the October 29 releases of US third-quarter GDP, Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation, and initial jobless claims. These reports will provide further information about economic growth, price pressures, and labor-market conditions.
The Bank of Japan’s monetary policy meeting on October 29–30 and the US midterm elections on November 3 are also on the calendar.
The Fed’s decision will depend on how policymakers assess persistent inflation alongside economic risks. Investors will look to the policy statement and Warsh’s press conference for a clearer indication of the central bank’s next steps.

high_priority_articles.summary: From the Mecca defence pact to Tehran talks: Is the Middle East’s security landscape shifting?  Euronews.comSaudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks  ReutersFlurry of Diplomacy in Iran Amid Reports of U.S. and Israeli Plans to Renew War  The New York TimesOil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate  CNBCMecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, ...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are pursuing talks with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of the Mecca Defence Alliance.
Senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are holding talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States continue.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are members of the Mecca Defence Alliance, a security alliance established amid regional instability and concerns over threats linked to Iran and its allies.
The three countries have now turned to direct talks with Tehran about regional security, even as the alliance faces growing pressure from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are attending the talks in Tehran on Monday, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.
They are reportedly meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has described the meeting as a potential step towards establishing cooperative regional security mechanisms.
Speaking at his weekly news conference in Tehran, Baghaei reiterated Iran’s longstanding call for what it describes as "endogenous security," a framework that would rely primarily on the capabilities and interests of regional countries.
The Mecca pact: collective defence against regional threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August 2026. Under the pact, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three, requiring the others to provide assistance.
The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia’s financial resources and influence in global energy markets, Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities and Turkey’s advanced defence industry and NATO membership.
Although the agreement was signed amid growing concerns over Iran and its allied groups, Turkish officials have insisted that it is not directed against Tehran or any other specific country.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an Aug. 8 interview with Anadolu that the agreement did not identify any country as a common threat. He explained that countries would not be considered targets unless they attacked a signatory.
The agreement has received approval in Pakistan, while Turkey has submitted it to parliament but has yet to complete the ratification process.
Houthi attacks put collective defence to the test
Escalating missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia have presented the Mecca alliance with its first major test.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries agreed to move towards implementing their collective defence commitments, including measures to ensure the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement published by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry.
Ankara, however, has drawn a line between supporting Saudi Arabia’s defences and joining offensive military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen.
At an Oct. 8 news conference in Ankara, Fidan said the agreement was defensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to another country to carry out attacks.
Turkey has instead been assessing possible contributions in areas such as air defence, electronic warfare and technical assistance.
The three nations are therefore pursuing direct engagement with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of an alliance designed to deter attacks on its members.
Why engage with Tehran?
Pakistan has played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington in recent months. Saudi Arabia is seeking to contain the threat posed by Houthi attacks on its territory and infrastructure, while Turkey has sought to prevent further regional escalation.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said in an Oct. 26 post on X that the Tehran visit was part of continued efforts by the Mecca pact countries to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
He said the talks were also intended to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan.
The Saudi statement suggests that talks with Iran are being pursued alongside the alliance’s defence commitments, rather than necessarily representing a fundamental change in the pact’s purpose.
Military deterrence or regional security?
Tehran’s emphasis on locally driven security arrangements appears, at least in principle, to share some common ground with the Mecca pact’s stated objective of strengthening security cooperation among regional states.
Significant differences remain, however.
Saudi Arabia maintains extensive security ties with the United States, Turkey is a NATO member, and Pakistan continues to pursue defence partnerships with several major powers.
Meanwhile, no agreement on a new joint regional security mechanism has been announced.
Nevertheless, the Tehran meeting highlights a notable development: Three countries that have established a mutual defence alliance in response to mounting regional security threats are now also pursuing direct dialogue with Iran.
The key question is whether this dual approach can have a lasting impact on regional tensions.

Summary
- South Korea’s Q3 GDP rose 1.0% q/q vs 0.7% expected as AI chip demand lifted exports and investment, with chips driving about half of growth. Private consumption fell for the first time in nearly four years. The KOSPI rally triggered a sidecar.
The strength of the beat, and the KOSPI sidecar on a sharp rally, underline how heavily Korean assets now trade on the AI chip cycle. That cuts both ways: it supports exporters and chip names while global AI demand holds up, but leaves the market exposed to any wobble in the global AI trade. The data reinforce the Bank of Korea’s hawkish bias after its July and September hikes, which should support the won and keep pressure on short-end bond yields. Weak consumption is the main argument against further tightening, so household-sensitive sectors are likely to keep lagging.
---
South Korea is riding the AI chip boom hard enough to set off market circuit-breakers, but its households are sitting this one out.
Summary:
- South Korea’s Q3 GDP grew 1.0% q/q, beating the 0.7% forecast and up from 0.6% in Q2; y/y growth was 3.4% versus 3.0% expected
- The Bank of Korea estimates semiconductors drive about half of growth; annual growth could reach 3.7% if Q4 holds at Q3 levels
- Exports rose 2.3% and facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by chip equipment
- Private consumption fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years, hit by a stock slump and auto strikes
- Exports topped $800 billion in January to September and are on track to pass $1 trillion this year
- The KOSPI’s strong rise triggered a sidecar halt on program trading
South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as the global AI chip boom lifted exports and investment, advance Bank of Korea estimates showed on Tuesday, though weak household spending marked a notable soft spot. Gross domestic product rose 1.0% from the previous quarter, beating the 0.7% median forecast in a Reuters poll and accelerating from 0.6% in the second quarter.
Korean equities rallied strongly on the session, with the move in the KOSPI triggering a sidecar, a temporary halt on program trading that the Korea Exchange applies when index futures move sharply, to cool momentum-driven orders.
The scale of the beat was striking against the central bank’s own expectations. The Bank of Korea had forecast 0.3% growth for the quarter in August, when it projected 3.3% growth for the year. If fourth-quarter output simply holds at third-quarter levels, annual growth would now come in at around 3.7%. A central bank official estimated that semiconductors are driving about half of the economy’s growth.
Exports rose 2.3% in the quarter on demand for chips, machinery and electrical equipment, while facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by semiconductor manufacturing equipment. South Korea’s exports topped $800 billion in the first nine months, already above last year’s full-year record, putting the country on track to become only the fourth to pass $1 trillion in a year, after the US, China and Germany.
The weak link is consumption. Private spending fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years, as financial services activity dropped amid a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers. The central bank expects a gradual recovery as chip firms’ dividend payouts in the fourth quarter and employee bonuses early next year lift household incomes, though one economist cautioned that a soft labour market and restrictive interest rates limit the scope for a strong rebound. Consumer sentiment also slipped in October.
The Bank of Korea held rates last week after back-to-back hikes in July and September but kept a hawkish stance, and today’s data give it little reason to soften that. On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4%, also above the 3.0% expected.

US Treasury yields decline
The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield slipped below 5%, reducing the dollar's advantage over the yen.
Investors expect the Federal Reserve to leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, although its guidance could influence currency movements.

Gold finished Friday at $3,997.48 an ounce, a weekly loss of 4.1% that says as much about forced selling as it does about sentiment. Behind that number sit two distinct pressures — a speculative retreat on the COMEX and a scramble for cash after a technology-stock rout — layered on top of an inflation-and-rates backdrop that has, for now, stripped the metal of its usual safe-haven bid.
Start with the futures market. CFTC positioning data as of Tuesday showed large speculators cutting their net long exposure, even as open interest initially rose 1.5%. The two moves together point to a market that wasn't uniformly walking away: small speculators were adding to longs while the big players trimmed. By Friday, open interest on COMEX had slipped to 400,538 contracts, down 0.2% week-on-week. That later decline may hint at a cooling in the unwinding, though it falls well short of proof that a floor is in place.
The liquidity story runs alongside it. Commerzbank analyst Carsten Fritsch points to gold sales aimed at covering equity losses and margin calls, with the selloff in technology and AI shares capable of triggering exactly such liquidations. Reuters reported the same dynamic. In this light, bullion is doing double duty — a hedge for some, a source of ready cash for others — and that second role explains part of the weakness without requiring any rethink of its long-term crisis credentials.
Why the Safe-Haven Trade Isn't Working
ING laid out the puzzle plainly on Friday: investors were fixated on expensive oil and what it might mean for inflation and central-bank policy. Gold therefore drew no benefit from lower US yields or from a flight to safety. The takeaway for holders is uncomfortable — geopolitical uncertainty on its own offers no dependable support right now. When higher energy costs entrench expectations of rates staying high for longer, that drag can outweigh the demand for protection.
CIBC Capital Markets, whose forecasts landed on Wednesday, still expects a recovery, just from a lower base and against less friendly monetary conditions than previously assumed. Analysts Anita Soni and Cosmos Chiu see gold at $4,500 an ounce in the fourth quarter of 2026 — above the latest close. They attribute their reduced projections to tighter policy, higher real yields and a firmer dollar. For 2027, the pair forecast an average price of $5,200; that annual figure should not be confused with the year-end target, nor read as a near-term call.
Official Buying and Indian Demand Offer a Counterweight
On the demand side, support hasn't vanished. The World Gold Council reports that China's central bank bought 23 tonnes in September, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. That official demand offsets some of the selling pressure, though it is no guarantee of an imminent turn — the recent price action shows central-bank buying and falling quotes can coexist comfortably.
The physical picture elsewhere is mixed. Indian gold purchases and premiums both picked up, according to Reuters, while Chinese jewellery demand stayed subdued. No broad-based surge in demand is visible.
Saxo Bank identifies near-term support at $3,970 an ounce. Only a move back above $4,230, in its view, would confirm the correction is over. That framing captures the distinction investors now face: a bounce would not be a confirmed reversal. As long as speculative buyers keep reducing positions and others need liquidity, physical demand is squaring off against substantial selling pressure. Whether inflation and rate worries keep the upper hand is the question that decides what comes next.

high_priority_articles.title: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Bolsonaro refuses to accept result: Early analysis from Chatham House experts - Chatham House
high_priority_articles.summary: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Bolsonaro refuses to accept result: Early analysis from Chatham House experts  Chatham House
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, has been re-elected president of Brazil for a fourth term. Lula secured 51.79 per cent of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.21 per cent.
The victory was a surprise: Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, led in the first round of the election held on 4 October. The result was announced after an unusual decision on Sunday by the country’s Supreme Court, which allowed polling centres to remain open longer than planned.
‘This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country’.
Defeated candidate Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, saying:
‘It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded.’
Below, Chatham House experts provide analysis of the meaning of the result for Brazilians, the region and the world.
1.    Dr Christopher Sabatini on what next for US relations?
2.    Dr Bruno Binetti on Brazil’s China policy
3.    Vanessa Rubio Marquez on the left and right in Latin America
4.    Luis Miguel Castilla Rubio on Lula’s policies and Brazil’s economy
What next for US relations?
Christopher Sabatini, Director of Chatham House’s Latin America Programme
As many waited for the administration of President Donald Trump to recognize President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s unexpected second-round presidential victory, other heads of state rushed to congratulate the Workers’ Party president’s victory over conservative Flávio Bolsonaro.
French President Emmanuel Macron, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney all publicly congratulated Lula on his victory. Even Brazil’s more conservative neighbours joined the chorus, including Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, Chilean President José Antonio Kast, and Paraguayan President Santiago Peña.
The White House’s hesitation is not surprising. It had been counting on the election of Bolsonaro to complete its bingo card of right-wing presidents in the Western Hemisphere, following a period of sustained electoral success for right-wing candidates stretching from Honduras to Argentina. But Latin American regional solidarity and respect for democratic institutions and the popular will trumped ideology and alignment with the US.
Adding Latin America’s largest democracy and economy would have represented a major victory for the self-proclaimed ‘Donroe Doctrine’. Instead, public support for Lula’s re-election may demonstrate that the bloc of Trump-aligned and Trump-adjacent presidents may not be as strong and ideological as many thought. (Only Argentine President Javier Milei has withheld congratulations for Lula.)
Meanwhile, Flávio continues to call for the annulment of the elections, claiming fraud – much as his father, Jair, did in 2022 when he lost to Lula. Part of his claim hinges on a Supreme Court justice who supported Lula’s Workers’ Party request to extend voting by two hours on Sunday.
That request was made originally by both parties to Brazil’s electoral court – in order to accommodate voters who struggled to make it to the booths due to heavy rains, and others allegedly affected by limited public transportation. But the decision to kick the request up to the Supreme Court after the electoral court failed to respond casts a pall over the results – and further threatens the reputation of a Supreme Court already under suspicion for being politicized.
Brazil’s modern, transparent voting system will be able to demonstrate the results – for those who want to believe them. But for core Bolsonaro supporters, trusting the results may be difficult. Flávio’s father also claimed unproven fraud in 2022. And father and son have baked distrust of the judicial and electoral system into their political DNA, polarizing politics and society in Brazil.
In the end, how far Flávio’s team decides to take its claims of fraud may depend on the White House and the US State Department. Both had a lot riding on a Bolsonaro victory. For Trump it would have been the crowning achievement for his support in the region, during this heavy year of presidential elections across the hemisphere.
For others the issue is more ideological and personal. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, like many Cuban-Americans, saw Lula’s Workers’ Party as complicit in upholding the communist regimes in Cuba and Nicaragua. Creating a ring of conservative, anti-communist governments across the hemisphere to stand with the US against those regimes has long been a dream of Republican administrations and Cuban-Americans in Florida. Their perspective will likely also help decide whether and when the Trump administration accepts a Lula victory.
With conservative majorities in both houses of Congress, Lula will have a difficult time attempting to tackle the economic and fiscal reforms necessary to keep the government solvent and address its looming sovereign debt. But the biggest loser in the election is social trust. The country’s voters are now almost evenly split between Bolsonaro and Lula (only 3.6 per cent separated the two leaders). And popular confidence in the Supreme Court may decline even more.
Will Lula change Brazil’s approach to China?
Bruno Binetti, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme
Lula’s re-election, following a campaign in which he declared that Brazil was ‘nobody’s backyard’ and denounced foreign interference, will be welcomed in Beijing.
China retains a close partner in Latin America’s largest economy, at a time when most countries in the region have moved closer to the Trump administration. Lula shares China’s commitment to a multipolar international order with a stronger role for the Global South. That includes efforts within BRICS to reduce reliance on the US dollar in international trade, reform global financial institutions and expand climate finance for developing countries.
This partnership is underpinned by strong economic ties – ties so important they would have endured a Bolsonaro victory. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009, driven by Brazilian exports of soybeans, iron ore and crude oil. In 2025, Brazilian exports to China reached $100 billion, compared with $38 billion to the US. This makes continued engagement with Beijing a priority for the powerful agribusiness sector, which is well represented in Congress and traditionally aligned with Bolsonaro and the political right.
Brazil was also the world’s largest recipient of Chinese investment in 2025, with Chinese firms expanding their presence in electricity infrastructure, manufacturing and mining. In the automotive sector, BYD and Great Wall Motor have established electric vehicle production facilities in Brazil, and Lula is pushing Chinese manufacturers to use more local suppliers and create jobs.
Brazil-China relations are likely to deepen during Lula’s fourth term, especially if the Trump administration continues to impose tariffs and other trade restrictions on Brazil.
Yet Lula is the ultimate pragmatist. He has always sought to maintain good relations with competing powers. Brazil and the US are already discussing a potential trade agreement that could include cooperation on critical minerals, a top priority for Washington as it tries to reduce dependence on China.
With the world’s second-largest rare-earth reserves, Lula is open to investment from both China and the US, provided it helps Brazil develop its own processing industries and move up the value chain,
What does this result mean for the left and right in Latin America?
Vanessa Rubio Marquez, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme
With Lula’s clear victory in the presidential run-off on 25 October, the two largest Latin American economies, Brazil and Mexico, will be perceived as the remaining guardians of the left, in a region that has largely flipped to the right of the political spectrum in recent years. However, the more relevant question is whether being left or right in the Western Hemisphere – and the world – still means what it once did.
Traditionally, the distinction between left and right was relatively clear. The left favoured a stronger role for the state in reducing inequality and redistributing wealth. The right, by contrast, placed greater emphasis on individual responsibility, private enterprise and preserving existing economic and social structures, accepting inequalities as a natural feature of society.
Today, these boundaries are being blurred. For instance, under Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil increased minimum monthly welfare transfers by 50 per cent (R$400 to R$600), reaching over 20 million families ahead of the 2022 election. And the reduction of the working week from 44 to 40 hours also took place under his mandate. Similar measures to protect specific sectors in society were implemented in Ecuador, where right-wing Daniel Noboa introduced financial assistance for vulnerable entrepreneurs.
However, the left -wing Mexican government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador limited pandemic spending and direct budget support to 0.7 per cent of GDP, compared with over 3 per cent across G20 emerging economies. And Chile’s left-wing president, Gabriel Boric, oversaw a 23.1 per cent real reduction in government spending in 2022.
Ever more, the extremes of left and right converge in pragmatic, immediate and populist policies. The more important divide is how governments exercise power, respect democratic institutions and protect individual freedoms while they deliver for the people.
A very interesting case of a tension between democracy and tangible results in matters that people prioritise is seen in El Salvador. President Nayib Bukele’s crackdown on gangs has brought major security gains, but at a cost to civil liberties. Emergency powers have been extended 55 times since 2022, with over 93,000 arrests and restrictions on due process.

high_priority_articles.title: Lula's reelection expected to bring continuity to China-Brazil ties, fresh momentum for Global South cooperation: expert - Global Times
high_priority_articles.summary: Lula's reelection expected to bring continuity to China-Brazil ties, fresh momentum for Global South cooperation: expert  Global Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (center) delivers a speech after winning the election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Photo: VCG
"Thank you, Brazilian people," Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva wrote on social media on Sunday night after securing a historic fourth presidential term in a dramatic electoral comeback.
When asked to comment on Lula's reelection victory and China's expectations for bilateral ties, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday that China takes note of the announcement by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court of President Lula's runoff victory and extends congratulations on that. China stands ready to work with Brazil to advance the building of the China-Brazil community with a shared future, he noted. 
Lula's victory has drawn international attention not only for its implications for Latin America's shifting political landscape, but also for the future of China-Brazil relations, with prospects for deeper economic cooperation, sustained high-level diplomatic engagement and closer coordination within BRICS and other multilateral frameworks coming into focus.
With 99.96 percent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.78 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.22 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally reported by Xinhua News Agency.
Lula will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, for a four-year term, marking his fourth election as Brazil's president.
The victory marked the first time a presidential candidate in Brazil had overturned a first-round deficit to win a runoff election. According to Xinhua, Brazil's presidential election follows a two-round majoritarian system. To win in the first round, held on October 4, a candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes. Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of incumbent Lula, winning about 47 percent of the valid votes against Lula's roughly 45 percent. As neither candidate crossed the 50-percent threshold, the two advanced to a runoff, which Lula won.
The election outcome comes amid significant political shifts across Latin America and growing geopolitical competition in the region. International media have highlighted the implications of Lula's victory for Brazil's relations with major powers, particularly China and the US, as well as the country's role in promoting cooperation among Global South nations.
The South China Morning Post reported on Monday that Lula's reelection would extend the tenure of an administration under which Chinese investment in Brazil had reached record levels. 
Pan Deng, director of the Latin America and Caribbean Region Law Center at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times on Monday that Lula's reelection has provided stability and predictability for China-Brazil relations over the next four years.
Pan said the political consensus reached by the two countries' leaders during Lula's 2023 visit to China, together with sustained high-level exchanges, has strengthened mutual trust and provided strategic guidance for bilateral ties. Despite potential constraints from a conservative Congress, cooperation with China enjoys broad support across Brazil's political spectrum and is unlikely to be significantly affected by domestic political divisions, he added.
China's top diplomat Wang Yi met with Special Advisor to the President of Brazil Celso Amorim on September 16 in Beijing. Amorim said Brazil stands ready to work with China to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state and inject new connotations into building a Brazil-China community with a shared future for a more just world and a more sustainable planet, Xinhua reported.
China has remained Brazil's largest trading partner for years, with bilateral economic ties forming a major pillar of the broader relationship.
Trade between Brazil and China reached a record $143.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026, reinforcing China's position as Brazil's largest trading partner. Brazilian exports to the Chinese market totaled $84.7 billion between January and September, an increase of 12 percent compared with the same period in 2025. Imports from China rose 9.9 percent to $58.6 billion.
The figures were released by Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services and compiled by the Brazil-China Business Council, according to a report published by Valor Econômico and covered by Brasil 247.
Looking ahead, Pan identified three areas with significant growth potential for China-Brazil cooperation: green and low-carbon development, including renewable energy and environmental protection; the digital economy and artificial intelligence, particularly in agriculture and AI governance; and expanded aerospace cooperation, building on the two countries' longstanding satellite partnership to advance remote-sensing applications in agriculture, disaster prevention and logistics.
Xu Shicheng, vice president of the China Society of Latin American Studies, told the Global Times on Monday that Lula's reelection could also help take China-Brazil relations to a new level, as bilateral cooperation has expanded beyond traditional commodity trade into emerging sectors such as electric vehicles, renewable energy, infrastructure and advanced technologies.
Beyond specific industries, Chinese analysts also pointed out that the Lula administration's emphasis on strategic autonomy and economic development aimed at improving people's livelihoods aligns closely with China's pursuit of high-quality development and open, inclusive international cooperation. At the multilateral level, Lula's reelection is also expected to provide continuity for Brazil's participation in BRICS and broader Global South cooperation, they noted.
China and Brazil could continue coordinating their positions on reform of the United Nations and World Trade Organization, global debt restructuring and international climate negotiations, helping ensure that global governance arrangements better reflect the concerns and development needs of emerging economies, Pan said.
The two countries could also jointly initiate inclusive cooperation projects targeting developing nations, providing additional opportunities for Global South countries to participate in international economic and technological cooperation. Pan said such initiatives could contribute to a more equitable international development environment and strengthen the collective voice of developing countries in global affairs.
The election has also attracted attention for its potential implications for Latin America's political landscape.
Reuters reported that Lula's victory came against the backdrop of recent electoral gains by right-wing political forces in several Latin American countries, raising questions about how Brazil's regional diplomacy might evolve during his next term.
Pan argued that Lula's victory should not simply be viewed as a return of a particular ideological camp, but rather as a pragmatic response by Brazilian voters to economic and social challenges, including high inflation and poverty pressures associated with neoliberal policies. The outcome could strengthen Latin America's pursuit of independent development and inject fresh momentum into regional integration, he said.
Xu noted that Lula could face considerable domestic political challenges during his fourth term, as right-wing and center-right forces secured significant representation in Brazil's Congress. Nevertheless, he said Lula's previous poverty alleviation and social welfare policies have retained support among lower-income voters, while his administration is expected to continue prioritizing BRICS cooperation and Brazil's role in the Global South.
The election also sends a message that Latin American countries can pursue development paths suited to their own national conditions rather than relying on Western-led models, while expanding diversified international partnerships, Pan said. He added that the result reflects growing regional aspirations for independent decision-making and resistance to external interference.

high_priority_articles.title: AfCFTA Chief Wamkele Mene Meets President Sassou Nguesso, Pushes for Greater Opportunities for Women and Youth in African Trade - pan african visions
high_priority_articles.summary: AfCFTA Chief Wamkele Mene Meets President Sassou Nguesso, Pushes for Greater Opportunities for Women and Youth in African Trade  pan african visions
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Ajong Mbapndah L
African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretary-General Wamkele Mene has held high-level talks with President Denis Sassou Nguesso of the Republic of Congo, as efforts intensify to accelerate continental economic integration, dismantle barriers to cross-border commerce and create greater opportunities for women and young entrepreneurs across Africa.
The meeting, held in Brazzaville on October 23, provided an opportunity for Mene to brief the Congolese leader on the state of AfCFTA implementation and discuss measures needed to translate Africa’s ambitious free trade agenda into tangible economic benefits for businesses and citizens.
The audience took place on the sidelines of the HerAfCFTA Regional Conference for Central Africa, held from October 21 to 23, bringing together policymakers, regional institutions, development partners and stakeholders committed to expanding women’s participation in intra-African trade.
Organised by the Government of the Republic of Congo in collaboration with the AfCFTA Secretariat, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS) Commission, the conference placed particular emphasis on empowering women entrepreneurs, improving access to African markets and strengthening regional economic cooperation.
At the heart of the discussions was a growing recognition that Africa’s economic integration ambitions will remain incomplete unless women and young people, who constitute a significant share of the continent’s entrepreneurial population, are equipped to participate meaningfully in the opportunities created by the continental free trade agreement.
In his closing remarks, Mene called for a practical action plan capable of delivering measurable results within the next 12 months, moving beyond policy commitments to concrete interventions that would strengthen businesses and expand trading opportunities.
Among the priorities outlined by the Secretary-General were improving market access for women- and youth-led enterprises, facilitating access to trade finance and harnessing digital technologies to connect African businesses with customers and commercial partners across national borders.
Access to finance remains a major obstacle for many African entrepreneurs, particularly women operating small and medium-sized enterprises. Mene stressed the importance of helping businesses become bankable and mobilising African development finance institutions to provide the resources required for expansion, investment and competitiveness.
He also underscored the need to dismantle structural and administrative barriers that continue to restrict women-led businesses from participating fully in regional and continental value chains.
The conference highlighted a proposal to establish a regional HerAfCFTA network in Central Africa, which would strengthen collaboration among women entrepreneurs, encourage knowledge sharing and create opportunities for businesses to develop partnerships across the region.
Such a network could provide an important platform for connecting women-owned enterprises with regional markets, financial institutions and trade support organisations, particularly in a region where fragmented markets, infrastructure gaps and complex cross-border procedures continue to constrain commercial activity.
Congo’s Visa-Free Initiative Draws Praise
A significant development during Mene’s visit was his endorsement of the Republic of Congo’s announced decision to introduce visa-free entry for African nationals beginning January 1, 2027.
The AfCFTA Secretary-General congratulated President Sassou Nguesso and his government on the initiative, recognising the importance of freer movement of people in facilitating business exchanges, investment and trade across the continent.
The announcement comes amid renewed calls for African governments to remove restrictions that complicate travel for entrepreneurs, investors and professionals seeking opportunities beyond their national borders.
While the AfCFTA seeks to establish a single African market for goods and services, the movement of businesspeople remains an essential component of its success. Visa restrictions, costly travel arrangements and cumbersome border procedures continue to undermine the ability of African enterprises to explore markets and establish commercial relationships.
Congo’s planned visa-free policy, if implemented as announced, could strengthen the country’s position as a destination for business engagement and regional economic cooperation while contributing to broader continental efforts to facilitate mobility.
For Central Africa, where regional integration has frequently faced logistical and regulatory challenges, measures that simplify movement between countries could provide additional momentum to efforts aimed at stimulating trade, tourism and investment.
Turning Africa’s Free Trade Ambitions into Results
The Brazzaville engagements also reinforced the importance of implementation as the AfCFTA moves from negotiated commitments toward the practical development of an integrated African market.
Designed to create one of the world’s largest free trade areas by participating countries, the AfCFTA offers African economies an opportunity to expand intra-continental commerce, stimulate industrialisation, strengthen regional value chains and reduce dependence on external markets.
However, achieving these objectives requires more than tariff reductions and trade agreements. Businesses must be able to access financing, obtain reliable market information, navigate customs procedures and transport their goods efficiently across borders.
For women entrepreneurs, these challenges are often compounded by limited access to capital, business networks and opportunities to participate in larger supply chains.
The HerAfCFTA initiative seeks to address some of these obstacles by placing women at the centre of the continent’s trade transformation and encouraging governments and institutions to develop policies that support their participation.
Mene’s emphasis on measurable results over the coming year reflects the need for stronger coordination between national governments, regional economic communities, financial institutions and development partners.
Digital trade was also identified as an important avenue for expanding opportunities, particularly for smaller enterprises that may lack the resources to establish a physical presence in multiple African markets.
By embracing digital platforms and technologies, African entrepreneurs could gain access to new customers, establish cross-border partnerships and participate more effectively in emerging continental value chains.
The AfCFTA Secretariat reaffirmed its commitment to working closely with governments, regional institutions and development partners to ensure that the priorities identified in Brazzaville translate into meaningful opportunities for women and young people.
For President Sassou Nguesso and the Republic of Congo, hosting the regional conference and receiving the AfCFTA Secretary-General placed Brazzaville at the centre of renewed discussions on the future of trade integration in Central Africa.
The engagements also highlighted the growing importance of political leadership in advancing continental economic integration, particularly as African countries seek to overcome longstanding obstacles to trade and investment.
As the AfCFTA implementation process gathers momentum, the message emerging from Brazzaville was clear: the success of Africa’s single market will ultimately be measured not only by agreements signed or policies adopted, but by the number of African businesses able to access new markets, attract investment, create jobs and compete successfully across the continent.
For women and young entrepreneurs, the challenge now is ensuring that the commitments made in Brazzaville produce the financing, partnerships and market opportunities needed to turn the promise of the AfCFTA into economic reality.

high_priority_articles.title: Epoch Raises $4.25 Million to Help SMEs Comply with EUDR Supply Chain Deforestation Regulation - ESG Today
high_priority_articles.summary: Epoch Raises $4.25 Million to Help SMEs Comply with EUDR Supply Chain Deforestation Regulation  ESG Today
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Supply chain intelligence platform Epoch announced today that it has raised $4.25 million in a seed funding round, alongside the launch of a new solution aimed at automating compliance for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), starting with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
According to Epoch, the funding and new launch come as businesses face increasing regulatory requirements to trace the origins of raw materials. The EUDR, for example, requires companies placing products including cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soy and wood on the EU market to demonstrate that they are deforestation-free and legally produced. The regulation will apply to large and medium-sized operators beginning December 30, 2026, and to most micro and small operators from June 30, 2027.
Founded in 2023 by CEO Jinal Surti and CTO William Ouellette, London-based Epoch develops AI-powered supply chain intelligence technology designed to help businesses trace raw materials to their origins and assess environmental and regulatory risks The company uses geospatial AI and automated research to analyze supply chains, reducing reliance on supplier questionnaires.
The company said that its technology identifies supplier facilities, locates plots where raw materials originate and assesses deforestation and legality risks. Its platform enables businesses to use the resulting information to address multiple regulatory requirements, including the EUDR.
According to Epoch, the new self-service solution allows SMBs to begin with existing supplier information and use AI assistants, including ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, to organize data and assess supply chain risks. The platform can generate Due Diligence Statements with supporting evidence for submission to the EU Information System (TRACES), the company added.
Surti said:
“We’ve built a compliance solution for the AI era. One sweep across a supply chain, using geospatial AI and agentic research, produces evidence that can be packaged for every regulation a company faces, including the ones not written yet. Enterprises get it inside the platforms they already run, and from today on, so does any SMB.”
The $4.25M seed round was led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River, and brings the total Epoch has raised to $6.26M. The company said that the new capital will go into product, infrastructure and the commercial team.
Christine Boyle, Partner, Burnt Island Ventures, said:
“Large companies rely on their supply chains to operate their businesses, and they are often operating in the dark as to the local conditions around drought, flood, and forest health. The Epoch platform leverages AI, earth observation data and proprietary models to enable visibility into risk mitigation, and compliance.”

high_priority_articles.title: France’s debt woes in focus as ECB meets - Kuwait Times
high_priority_articles.summary: France’s debt woes in focus as ECB meets  Kuwait Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
FRANKFURT: France’s deteriorating public finances will take centre stage when the European Central Bank meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone’s second-biggest economy just yet. The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Thursday’s meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis,” said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics. French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year’s budget, which aims to reduce the country’s vast debts.
Concerns have also been fuelled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combating sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields. However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France’s problems do not meet the threshold. The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted” moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading—but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France’s finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea. Asked about France’s rising yields earlier this month, she responded: "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies.”
France’s central bank chief, who sits on the ECB’s governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met” for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France” at Thursday’s meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5 percent. The ECB’s rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the US central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September. Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8 percent in September, although closely watched core inflation—excluding volatile energy and food prices—hardly changed. There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices,” ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France’s crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike,” he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB’s task”. Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year. She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos. But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB’s last meeting in September there was "nothing to report” on the matter. --AFP

high_priority_articles.summary: Britain To Unveil Plan To Meet NATO Defence Spending Targets By 2035  Arise News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government will outline a plan to fully fund its existing defence commitments and meet its NATO spending targets by 2035.
Burnham said Finance Minister John Healey would provide details of the funding plan on Wednesday when he delivers his first budget, as the defence industry seeks assurances that Britain has a clear strategy for increasing military spending.
Speaking on ITV’s Good Morning Britain on Monday, Burnham said the government’s immediate priority was to fully fund its previously announced defence investment plan.
“We’ve been working hard to do that,” he said. “It’s crucial that we have a funded plan that we can then implement, and we will set out more details on Wednesday as to how we’ve done that.”
Asked whether the plan would include increasing defence spending to three per cent of gross domestic product by 2030 and 3.5 per cent by 2035, Burnham confirmed that the targets would be included.
“It is, and we will set out a plan as to how we think is the right way to do that,” he said, adding that Britain would meet its NATO commitments.
Britain currently spends about 2.6 per cent of its GDP on defence and has previously pledged to reach the three per cent target during the next parliamentary term. The country’s next general election is due by mid-2029 at the latest.
Last year, NATO members agreed to spend 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence requirements by 2035, alongside an additional 1.5 per cent on broader defence and security measures.
The British defence industry has called for a clear and gradual increase in military spending, warning that delaying the planned rise until after 2030 could undermine the country’s credibility with allies and investors.

high_priority_articles.summary: UK PM Andy Burnham signals youth jobs support changes as John Healey prepares NATO spending plan  Business Upturn
high_priority_articles.full_text:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has signalled changes to government support for young people seeking work, saying savings could be made while improving how employment assistance is delivered. He has also confirmed that Defence Secretary turned finance minister John Healey will set out the government's plan for meeting its NATO commitments on Wednesday.
The two announcements come ahead of the UK government's budget on October 28, when ministers are expected to explain how they intend to manage public spending while addressing youth unemployment and national security.
Burnham has made helping young people into employment a priority for his government. At the same time, his administration faces pressure to meet defence spending commitments without putting additional strain on public finances.
The upcoming budget is expected to provide more detail on how the government plans to balance these competing priorities.
Andy Burnham signals changes to youth employment support
Burnham has indicated that the government's approach to supporting young people who are out of work needs to change. He also suggested that money could be saved by reviewing how existing support is provided.
The issue is significant for the UK, where youth unemployment and the number of young people outside education, employment or training have become major policy concerns.
Government figures cited in recent reporting show that close to one million people aged between 16 and 24 are classified as not in education, employment or training. The group is commonly referred to as NEET.
Burnham has argued that the government should invest in helping young people develop skills and find jobs instead of relying primarily on benefits after they struggle to enter the workforce.
His approach places greater emphasis on employment opportunities, training and practical assistance. The aim is to help young people move into work while reducing long-term dependence on government support.
However, changes to youth employment programmes could raise questions about which services will receive funding and how any savings will be achieved. Burnham's latest remarks indicate that the government wants to review the current system, but the precise changes and their financial impact will depend on the details announced by ministers.
The budget could therefore offer a clearer picture of how the government intends to support young jobseekers while controlling expenditure.
John Healey to outline Britain's NATO spending commitments
Burnham has also confirmed that John Healey will set out the government's path towards meeting Britain's NATO defence spending commitments on Wednesday.
The announcement is important because the government faces pressure to explain how it will finance the country's military requirements over the coming years. NATO allies have agreed to a higher long-term defence spending target, increasing the importance of clear funding plans.
According to Reuters, the UK government intends to outline a pathway towards allocating 3.5% of gross domestic product to core defence spending by 2035. The budget is expected to explain how Britain plans to work towards that commitment.
The challenge is finding the money while maintaining the government's other spending priorities. Burnham has previously stressed that national security must be protected without ignoring social security needs.
Healey's budget will therefore be closely watched by defence officials and policymakers looking for clarity on future military investment. A clear spending pathway could provide greater certainty about the resources available to the armed forces and the timetable for meeting NATO's targets.
Wednesday's budget will test the government's spending priorities
The youth employment announcement and the NATO spending plan highlight two major challenges facing Burnham's government: improving opportunities for young people and maintaining Britain's defence commitments.
Both priorities require funding, but the government also has to manage borrowing and meet its wider fiscal objectives. That makes decisions about departmental budgets and potential savings particularly important.
The government has indicated that existing resources will need to be used carefully, with new commitments requiring decisions about spending elsewhere. The budget is expected to show how that approach will work in practice.
For young people, the key question is whether changes to employment support will create clearer routes into work and training. For the defence sector, attention will focus on whether Healey provides a credible timetable for meeting Britain's NATO obligations.
Wednesday's budget should offer the first detailed indication of how Burnham and Healey intend to bring those priorities together. The figures and policy measures announced will determine whether the government's promises are matched by a practical funding plan.

high_priority_articles.title: Sovereignty and scale: How industry Is delivering ‘Made in NATO’ - EU Reporter
high_priority_articles.summary: Sovereignty and scale: How industry Is delivering ‘Made in NATO’  EU Reporter
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The security of the world is at a critical juncture. The conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East and tensions in the Indo-Pacific are only part of the challenge. At precisely the moment we face a renewed great power competition, we may be less equipped than ever to meet it, writes George Whittier, CEO Fairbanks Morse Defense.
Decades of post-Cold War military downsizing have hollowed out defence industrial capacity across Europe and the United States. Euro-Atlantic governments are now realising that they must rapidly rebuild their industrial bases to address a complex geopolitical environment. Defence spending in Europe has grown by 90% nominally since 2022 and the U.S. 2027 defence budget is expected to top €1.3 trillion ($1.5 trillion). Across the NATO alliance, members are signing contracts for equipment that industry is struggling to produce at the speed of need. The weak point is not demand, it’s the capacity to meet demand.
This tension is especially clear in the maritime domain. The largest shipyards in Europe and the United States are currently reporting tens of billions of euros in backlogs along with a shortage of skilled labour and aging port infrastructure. According to the European Commission, manufacturing output has grown by a mere 1% for frigates and 7% for attack submarines over the last decade. Meanwhile, Russia is maintaining a steady pace of warship construction, despite crippling western sanctions, and China produces roughly the equivalent tonnage of the entire French Navy every four years.
While the focus of NATO members has been on strategic autonomy, the fact is that no nation on its own has the industrial capacity to confront the geopolitical crises at hand. The days when strategic industrial capacity was centered on a broad supplier base of tens to thousands of machine shops and suppliers is gone. Industry is now playing a vital role in reviving it.
The challenge of reviving the allied defence industrial base has been a central theme of recent NATO summits. The war in Ukraine, which triggered a survival instinct amongst members, has helped catalyse increased cooperation between members and industry. The Defense Production Act Plan and Industrial Capacity Expansion Pledge, initiated in 2023 and 2024, created a framework for joint procurement and increased interoperability to achieve production at scale across the alliance. The Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation (SYNC), signed by heads of state in Ankara this year, further emphasised the importance of industry in collective security and deterrence, as did the announcement of $54 billion in allied defence procurement. As NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rightly said, these “Made in NATO” capabilities represent “transatlantic cooperation in action.”
Sovereignty, however, is a sticking point. Many allies are concerned that NATO is dominated by the United States. According to European Parliamentary Research Service reports, three-quarters of European defence procurement now flows to non-European suppliers, and more than half of that is to the United States. At a time of heightened global conflict, EU nations and the UK fear that a NATO-integrated supply chain will leave them structurally dependent on, or dominated by, America, and therefore vulnerable to crises, disruptions or political-economic disputes. But allied production is not either-or, it’s all of the above.
Nations do not have to choose between sovereignty and the ability to defend themselves. Allies must build more of their own defence capacity, not just for NATO, but to support sovereign military demand and national economic strength. A go-it-alone approach is not tenable for either side of the Atlantic. In fact, nationally-isolated procurement strategies have left Europe's defence industry fragmented, especially smaller, specialized suppliers critical to naval construction. This fragmentation is the enemy of scale. It is why NATO has increasingly stepped into its role as an aggregator of demand, providing standards and requirements for interoperability and a multinational buy signal so suppliers can serve a broader, more predictable market.
When I emphasise that we are better off working together, I speak from experience. Two months ago, the company I lead broke ground on a manufacturing centre of excellence in the Słupsk region in Poland. Working in partnership with the local government, and using the advanced engineering of our Norwegian subsidiary, the new centre will increase annual production of handling equipment for allied autonomous and crewed vessels by up to 80%. Opening this facility allows us to tap into a skilled workforce in Europe, in a strategic location for Europe, to provide NATO and European forces with the equipment they need to defend themselves.
Ultimately, countries should control the capabilities and decisions essential to their security. They also need equipment delivered at speed. Allied production can help achieve both if nations identify clearly which capabilities must be local and which can be complementary and accessed from close partners.
A nation doesn't need to be able to build a warship or platform end-to-end to have a thriving defence sector. Shoring up the NATO arsenal depends on expanding the capacity and depth of allied suppliers. By specialising in critical ship equipment and plugging those components into the broader allied market, local economies gain larger, steadier demand than any single domestic government could ever guarantee on its own.

high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's Q3 Growth Hits 1.0%, Driven by Semiconductor Exports  조선일보
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea’s economic growth rate in the third quarter significantly surpassed expectations for the third consecutive quarter, driven by sustained increases in semiconductor exports amid the U.S.-led AI (artificial intelligence) boom. The Bank of Korea announced on the 27th that the economy grew by 1.0% quarter-on-quarter in its “Third Quarter Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP)” report. This figure is more than three times the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3%. Year-on-year growth reached 3.4%, also exceeding the projected 2.6%. If this momentum continues through year-end, annual growth could approach 4%, far surpassing the Bank of Korea’s forecast of 3.3%. Lee Dong-won, head of the Bank of Korea’s Economic Statistics Division 2, stated, “If fourth-quarter growth remains at the current level, annual growth would reach approximately 3.9%. A quarter-on-quarter growth rate of 1.4% or higher would enable annual growth of 4%.”
Similar to the first and second quarters, exports grew by 2.3% quarter-on-quarter, led by semiconductors and other IT items, marking a higher increase than the second quarter’s 1.3%. Year-on-year export growth was 8.6%, slightly lower than the second quarter’s 8.9%. Equipment investment increased by 4.1% quarter-on-quarter and 9.4% year-on-year, driven by rising semiconductor facility investments. Lee Dong-won explained, “Semiconductors accounted for roughly half of the overall growth.”
Despite strong export-driven growth, private consumption declined by 0.2% quarter-on-quarter, marking the first decrease since the fourth quarter of 2022, during the COVID-19 pandemic. In the second quarter, private consumption had risen by 0.4% due to improved consumer sentiment from a stock market rally and increased home appliance purchases from Samsung Electronics’ gift certificate redemption event. However, these effects dissipated in the third quarter. Lee Dong-won noted, “Declines in financial service consumption due to reduced stock trading volumes and delayed car deliveries from automaker strikes contributed to the drop. Private consumption is expected to rebound in the fourth quarter due to semiconductor company dividends and performance-based bonuses in early 2024, which will boost household income.”
The Bank of Korea explained, “Consumption of goods like passenger vehicles and home appliances, as well as services such as finance and dining, all decreased.” Year-on-year private consumption growth was 1.1%. Government consumption increased by 1.9% quarter-on-quarter and 2.6% year-on-year, driven by higher spending on goods, health insurance benefits, and other expenses.
The third-quarter real gross domestic income (GDI), which reflects export prices, rose by 3.4% quarter-on-quarter as AI-driven demand surged, pushing semiconductor prices higher. While this was a slight decline from the previous quarter’s 3.7%, it remained over three times the GDP growth rate. Year-on-year GDI growth reached 18.8%, the highest since the fourth quarter of 1977, up from the previous quarter.
While GDP measures domestic production, GDI is calculated by adjusting export prices relative to import prices. Despite rising oil import costs due to the Middle East conflict, semiconductor export prices increased more sharply, sustaining high GDI growth. The year-on-year GDI growth rate exceeded the GDP growth rate by 15.4 percentage points, marking the third consecutive quarter of record-breaking gaps.
With inflation persistently above the Bank of Korea’s 2% target and strong growth continuing into the third quarter, the likelihood of additional interest rate hikes before year-end has increased. The central bank paused its rate hikes on the 22nd after raising rates twice in July and August. Governor Shin Hyun-song views the semiconductor-driven growth as a demand-side inflationary factor. At a post-meeting press conference, he stated, “Given that growth and inflation trends are stronger than August projections, maintaining the current tight monetary policy stance is necessary.” The final Monetary Policy Board meeting of the year is scheduled for November 26.
