high_priority_articles.title: From 24 GPUs to 4: Three South Korean Startups Shaking Up the AI Chip Game - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: From 24 GPUs to 4: Three South Korean Startups Shaking Up the AI Chip Game  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
As artificial intelligence (AI) computing costs emerge as corporate America's biggest burden, South Korean startups that are shaking up the market along a different axis from the chip performance race are drawing attention. The protagonists are Nota, Lablup and MangoBoost, which respectively handle model lightweighting, graphics processing unit (GPU) resource allocation and data center infrastructure efficiency.
The most eye-catching result came from Nota. The company cut the number of Nvidia B300 GPUs needed to run Alibaba's 2.4-trillion-parameter Qwen 3.8 model from 24 to four. It also reduced H100 GPU usage on Upstage's Solar Open 2 from eight to two. The gains come from combining quantization, which lowers a model's computational precision, with pruning, which cuts away low-importance parts. At an International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) competition, it placed in the top ranks by boosting the inference speed of the 4-billion-parameter Qwen 3.5 model roughly sevenfold on a single Nvidia A10G GPU.
Lablup handles the area of sharing GPUs among multiple users. Its Backend.AI platform pools scattered GPUs into a single resource and automatically allocates as much as each task needs. It manages simultaneous training and inference by multiple users so that jobs do not collide, allowing companies to raise utilization rates without buying additional equipment. The company has also joined DGX Ready, Nvidia's technology partner program.
MangoBoost raises efficiency at the level of the entire data center. Building on more than a decade of data processing unit (DPU) research by Seoul National University researchers, it supplies the GPU server Alfonso, the storage server Caesar and the inference software LLM Boost as a package. Its strength is optimizing hardware and software simultaneously without being tied to a specific semiconductor vendor, and it is also working with AMD.
Some ask whether the spread of efficiency technology will reduce semiconductor demand. The industry's judgment leans the opposite way. The argument is that as the cost of using AI falls, services and users will multiply and total computing volume may actually grow. Global consulting firm McKinsey projected that about 60% of total AI computing demand in 2030 will come from inference. Market research firm TrendForce analyzed that an efficient AI model can process up to six times as many tokens on the same accelerator configuration as an existing large model.
SK Hynix also said in its second-quarter earnings announcement that "the emergence of high-efficiency AI models will not necessarily lead to a reduction in AI infrastructure investment." Its judgment is that the AI market itself grows because more users can use a wider variety of services on the same infrastructure. Because memory bandwidth, which supplies data quickly during inference, remains a bottleneck, the importance of high-performance, high-capacity memory is preserved even as GPU computing performance rises.
This trend could lead memory makers to expand their product lines. Demand need not stay confined to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for training but can broaden to server DRAM, low-power memory and enterprise solid-state drives (eSSD). As agentic AI and on-device AI spread, memory demand for smartphones, PCs, cars and robots is also expected to grow.
A change in how memory itself is designed is another variable. When the custom HBM market — customer-tailored HBM — opens in earnest next year, the scope of competition for memory makers shifts from storage capacity and speed to the performance and power efficiency of the entire AI system. If HBM is likened to an apartment building, the upper floors are the space that stores data, and the approach is to put customer-requested functions into the "base die" — the first floor that exchanges data with external AI chips. Nvidia's NVHBM, unveiled in August, centers on moving the memory control circuitry found in existing AI accelerators into the base die.
Ahn Hyun, head of development at SK Hynix and a president of the company, said in a keynote speech at the SEDEX semiconductor exhibition on the 14th that "standard HBM and custom HBM will coexist, but over the long term the custom trend will expand further." Because custom HBM reflects each customer's design requirements, its unit price is higher than standard products, making it an opportunity for memory makers to widen a high-value-added market.
The more customized design expands, however, the greater the tension over who leads design and production. Because the space for customer-specific circuitry must be decided jointly, memory makers must implement their own circuitry in a smaller area. It is in the same context that a plan is being discussed to have the base die that Samsung Electronics has produced in its own foundry made instead at rival TSMC, in line with Nvidia's requirements. If other AI chip developers such as AMD and Broadcom later demand TSMC processes as well, a structure could spread in which memory makers secure orders but leave production of core components to outside parties. That is why some argue that the mix of standard and custom products must be adjusted in light of per-customer profitability and dependence on specific foundries.
In the end, the competitive axis of the semiconductor market is shifting from the performance of a single chip to an optimization ecosystem spanning models, hardware and infrastructure. As the view spreads that simply adding more high-performance GPUs cannot keep up with surging computing demand and cost burdens, technology that bridges the gap between models and hardware is taking shape as an independent industry. The question is whether, while chipmakers and model developers focus on the performance race, the technology of the South Korean startups connecting the two can be evaluated in the global market as an alternative.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eases 0.1%
[SYDNEY] Share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday (Oct 26) as oil eased from six-month highs ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings and company earnings that will further test investor confidence in the artificial intelligence boom.
Brent oil slipped 1 per cent to US$115.48 amid reports Qatari mediators were in Teheran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the US.
Brent futures jumped 6.2 per cent last week to their highest weekly close since mid-2022 as Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over energy supplies. US crude futures fell 1.1 per cent to US$102.08 a barrel.
Japan’s Nikkei dipped 0.8 per cent, after losing 4 per cent last week, while South Korea fell 0.4 per cent, having shed almost 19 per cent so far in October. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1 per cent.
The inflationary pulse from oil is likely to alarm all the central banks meeting this week, with hikes seen as just a matter of time even if some hold for now.
“The main message from global central banks grappling with 2026’s macroeconomic surprises is that a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway,” said Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan.
“G3 central banks are likely to remain on hold, but Canada should start its tightening cycle and first moves are expected from the UK and Sweden (in September).”
New Zealand’s central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US Federal Reserve will stand pat, but imply an 80 per cent chance it will pull the trigger in December. Much the same is priced in for the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank.
A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1 per cent in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2 per cent annualised pace thanks in part to furious spending on data centres.
“The Fed is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting but is likely to deliver a second hike in December,” analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note.
“The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran,” they added.
“The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden.”
Hyperscalers to test AI hype
On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures both edged up 0.2 per cent. In Europe, Eurostoxx 50 futures firmed 0.2 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.1 per cent.
Earnings highlights will include the hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, among one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting. Results from Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade.
Consensus on Microsoft is for US$90.6 billion of revenue and an adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of US$4.73, with Amazon at US$202 billion of revenue and EPS around US$1.97. Alphabet revenue is seen at US$128 billion and EPS of US$3.00.
Equity valuations have been tested by higher bond yields, though Treasuries did manage a rally last week before running into renewed selling on Friday.
Yields on 10-year Treasuries were at 5 per cent, but off a peak of 5.36 per cent hit early in October.
In currency markets, the Japanese yen retained its safe-haven appeal at 157.00 per US dollar, having gained around 0.8 per cent last week.
The euro held steady at US$1.1204 as political unrest in France kept investors wary, though the country did escape a credit downgrade last week.
Sterling held at US$1.3346 with Britain’s new finance minister, John Healey, set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war.
The Brazilian real was yet to trade in Asia as Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country’s electoral court said.
In commodity markets, non-interest bearing gold was a fraction firmer at US$4,001 an ounce, having fallen more than 4 per cent last week. REUTERS

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday.
Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.
Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department.
"Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.
In September, the Fed raised — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with of gas, food, and other expenses.
Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.
According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).
In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs.
"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, a week after it was announced by US First Lady, Melania Trump.
The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.
Oleshky is on the south bank of the river Dnipro, which forms the front line in the Kherson region. The remaining residents have been desperately short of food and other essential supplies.
Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.
The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured the ceasefire in Oleshky.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she said in a press release.
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The Chinese-owned online retailer has promised stronger action to address several violations of the EU’s Digital Services Act, the European Commission said on Monday, following a €200 million fine in May.
The European Commission has said it has accepted Temu's action plan to address several violations of the bloc's Digital Services Act (DSA).
Temu has promised to carry out a risk analysis, to keep a close eye on measures to prevent the sale of illegal products on its platform and to step up its efforts if needed.
The Chinese retailer will also review how its recommender systems "may amplify the spread of illegal goods", the Commission said.
In May this year, Temu was fined €200 million by the EU for allowing the sale of illegal products like dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers on its platform.
The fine came after a formal investigation launched in October 2024 into whether Temu was meeting its obligations as a designated Very Large Online Platform under the EU's Digital Services Act.
Commission investigators said the platform failed to properly identify and address the risks posed by illegal and unsafe products sold to European consumers.
Today, Temu welcomed the approval of its action plan by European regulators. “We appreciate the Commission's constructive engagement with us throughout the process,“ the company said in a statement.
The plan "stands as a clear testament to Temu's commitment to investing in robust compliance infrastructure to ensure a safe, trustworthy shopping environment for all EU users”, it added.
The Chinese retail giant has 130 million users in the 27-nation EU, nearly a third of the bloc's population, making it one of the biggest online retailers in Europe.
Temu is one of several ecommerce platforms dealing with the EU’s new €3 fees on low-value packages since July, while those worth less €150 had entered the bloc duty free beforehand.
The new packaging rules have seen imports, especially from China, slump by 30% to 40% since coming into force.
